item.title: Negotiating a lease renewal
item.context_text: You have rented a one-bedroom flat in Istanbul for two years while working for a software company. You have always paid on time and looked after the flat. Your landlord has just sent a notice proposing a significant rent increase for the next year, and you would like to stay, but not at that price.
item.objective_text: Understand the notice and your options, learn the landlord's real position, write a reasoned counter-offer, and negotiate a compromise on the phone.
item.target_grammar: conditionals and concessions for negotiation (If you were willing to…, I'd be prepared to…; While I understand…, …)
item.cultural_note: Landlords often value a reliable long-term tenant more than a slightly higher rent, because an empty flat and a new tenant both cost money. Framing your offer around reliability and commitment is usually more persuasive than simply saying the increase is unfair. Tenancy rules differ by country, so check the local regulations before you negotiate.
success_conditions: Identify the proposed terms and the response deadline
Negotiate on the phone and agree clear terms

children.title: Read the renewal notice
children.instructions: Read the notice from your landlord. Then answer the questions.
children.prompt_text:
Dear Tenant,
Your current lease ends on 31 May. I would be happy to renew it for a further twelve months. Due to rising maintenance and property costs, the new monthly rent would be increased by 25%, payable from 1 June.
Please confirm by 30 April whether you wish to renew on these terms. If I do not hear from you by then, I will assume you intend to leave at the end of the current lease and will begin advertising the flat.
Kind regards,
Mr Demir

questions.prompt: What reason does the landlord give for the increase?
options: A new tenant has offered more
questions.explanation: "Due to rising maintenance and property costs."

questions.prompt: What happens if you don't reply by 30 April?
options: The lease renews automatically at the old rent
The landlord will assume you are leaving
questions.explanation: "I will assume you intend to leave at the end of the current lease and will begin advertising the flat."

children.title: Listen to the landlord
children.instructions: You meet Mr Demir on the stairs and he talks to you briefly. Listen. Then answer the questions.
children.prompt_text: Ah, hello! You got my letter? I know, I know, it's a big jump. To be honest with you, it's not really about the money from you. The building needs a new roof next year, and the bank wants me to show steady income from the flats. The last thing I want is the flat empty for two months while I look for someone new. You've never been late once. If you could commit for a longer period, maybe we could talk about the number.

questions.prompt: What does the landlord most want to avoid?
questions.explanation: "The last thing I want is the flat empty for two months while I look for someone new."

questions.prompt: What does he hint he would accept in exchange for a lower increase?
questions.explanation: "If you could commit for a longer period, maybe we could talk about the number."

questions.prompt: Why does he need steady income?
options: The bank wants to see it before the roof work
questions.explanation: "The building needs a new roof next year, and the bank wants me to show steady income."

children.title: Write your counter-offer
children.instructions: Reply to Mr Demir in writing before the deadline. Acknowledge his situation, remind him of your record as a tenant, and make a specific counter-offer that uses what you learned on the stairs.
children.prompt_text:
To: Mr Demir
Subject: Lease renewal – flat 7
children.goal: Make a reasoned, specific counter-offer that meets both sides' interests.

points.label: mention your record as a tenant

children.model_answer:
Dear Mr Demir,
Thank you for your letter and for explaining the situation with the roof when we spoke. I'd very much like to stay in the flat. While I understand that your costs have risen, a 25% increase is more than I can manage. Over the past two years I have always paid on time and kept the flat in good condition, and I would be happy to offer you more stability: if you were willing to limit the increase to 10%, I would be prepared to sign a two-year fixed-term lease. That would guarantee your income for the bank and avoid any empty months.
Best regards,
Anvar Rashidov

children.title: Agree terms on the phone
children.instructions: Mr Demir calls. He proposes a middle figure. Respond: weigh up his offer, propose or accept a final compromise, and confirm the terms clearly so there is no misunderstanding.
children.prompt_text: Mr Demir: I read your email. Ten per cent is too low for me, but I like the idea of two years. What would you say to fifteen?
children.goal: Reach a compromise and confirm the terms precisely.

points.label: link it to the longer lease

children.model_answer: Thank you for considering it. Fifteen is still quite a stretch for me, but I'd like to find a middle ground. Could we meet at twelve per cent for a two-year fixed lease? If that works for you, then just to confirm: twelve per cent from the first of June, fixed for twenty-four months. Could you send me the new contract in writing so I can sign it this week?
